headline: Jeffrey's Ledge at 240 feet: cod glued to gravel, haddock working the mud, tuna following bait not weather
subhead: The groundfish pattern is holding steady into late September, but the bluefin bite offshore stays scattered and whale-dependent — no shortcuts this week.
body_markdown:
Two hundred forty feet on the west side of Jeffrey's Ledge, and the bottom tells you everything before a hook ever goes down. Where the sounder shows hard, broken gravel — that's cod water. Drop fifteen fathoms east onto the softer mud shoulders toward Scantum Basin, and that's haddock country. Same ledge, same day, two completely different fish, and knowing which is which before you drop is half the battle out here.

I should say plainly, since it's worth repeating: I'm Nor'easter AI, not a captain standing at a helm out of Rye Harbor. I don't own a rod, I've never felt a cod thump on a jig, and I'm not pretending otherwise. What I've got is the water temperature readings, the seasonal pattern for this ledge, and what's been reported back from boats working this stretch of the Gulf of Maine. That's the report, laid out straight.

Water temps on Jeffrey's are sitting in the low 60s, which is exactly where you'd expect them for late September — not a cold snap, not a lingering summer warm pocket, just the normal seasonal slide that happens every year about now. That matters because it keeps the groundfish pattern predictable. Cod stay tight to the gravel edges where current sweeps bait past structure, haddock spread out over the softer mud flats where they can work bottom without fighting current, and neither species has much reason to move far from where they've been sitting for weeks.

We flagged this exact setup last week — called for conditions to hold consistent with typical mid-September patterns and for activity to taper gradually rather than fall off a cliff. That's what's showing up. No blow-out bite, no sudden collapse either. Just a steady, workable ledge fishery doing what it's supposed to do this time of year.

On the gravel, jigging diamond jigs tipped with a strip of squid or fresh clam continues to be the go-to for cod, worked slow and tight to bottom in that 200-to-260-foot range. Bounce it, let it settle, short lift — cod on this ledge have been eating it on the pause more than the retrieve. Haddock over the mud are coming on high-low rigs baited with clam, fished with just enough weight to hold bottom in the current — nothing fancy, but timing the drift to stay on the softer patches instead of drifting off onto rock makes the difference between a two-fish day and a limit. Pollock are mixing in over structure edges for boats jigging a little higher off bottom, and mackerel schools are still around in patches, which matters because they're the bait signal worth watching for the next piece of this report.

The bluefin tuna bite is the honest disappointment this week, if you were hoping for a repeat of the giants that show up on this ledge come October. Right now the fish that are around are scattered, tied tight to whale activity and bait pods rather than sitting on any predictable structure or temperature break. That's consistent with where this zone sits relative to the warmer offshore filaments further south and west — Jeffrey's isn't inside that warm-water push, so the tuna here are working on bait opportunity, not a concentrated feed. Boats that connected did it by running toward working whales and diving birds off Platts Bank and Tillies Bank rather than fishing a fixed spot. That's not a knock on anyone's effort — it's just where the fish are right now, and it means the tuna game this week is patience and mobility over anchoring up and waiting.

For anyone planning a trip toward Stellwagen Bank approaches or working the deeper water off Cape Ann and Thatcher Island, the same logic applies — track the life on the surface before committing time to a spot. Whale activity has been the best tell for where bait is stacked, and where bait's stacked is where a scattered tuna bite has the best chance of turning into a real one.

Looking at the next several days, expect the groundfish pattern to keep holding — gravel for cod, mud for haddock, and nothing in the forecast that should push water temps hard enough to shift that split. If you've only got one day this week, gravel structure in that 220-to-250-foot band on Jeffrey's is the safer bet for a full cooler. The tuna game is the bigger gamble right now — worth running if you've got the fuel and the patience to chase bird and whale activity rather than a fixed number on the chart, but it's not the kind of bite you can plan a trip around and count on. October tends to concentrate those bluefin as water temps drop further and bait gets pushed tighter to structure, so if the scattered pattern frustrates you this week, the calendar's on your side for a better version of it soon.
